The letter H is never pronounced. Ho = "o", hai = "ai", ha = "a", hanno = "anno" (with a double "n"). H is there only to distinguish "ho" (I have) from "o" (or).
GLI is a soft "ly": figlio = "fi-lyo", famiglia = "fa-mi-lya", gli = "lyi". The tongue presses against the roof of the mouth.
Z is read "ts" (grazie = "gra-tsye") or "dz" (zero = "dzero"). Double, it's held longer: pizza = "pit-tsa".
Watch the double consonants in numbers: otto (8), sette (7), diciassette (17), diciotto (18). And the accent in "ventitré".
AVERE is the second important verb, after ESSERE. The forms with H are read without the H.
Good news for Romanians: "ho, hai, ha" look like "am, ai, are". And as in Romanian, the pronoun isn't required: "Ho una sorella" = "I have a sister".
2. Age: with AVERE, as in Romanian
In Italian, age is expressed with AVERE, just as in Romanian: "am 29 de ani" = "ho 29 anni". No "of"!
Don't translate Romanian "de" in "29 de ani": correct is "ho 29 anni", not "ho 29 di anni".
3. The definite article: il, lo, la, l', i, gli, le
Unlike Romanian, where the article is attached at the end (casa, fratele), in Italian the article comes BEFORE, as a separate word. Its form depends on gender and the first letter of the word.
before z, s + consonant, gn, ps, y
To start with, remember the basic rule: masculine = il / i, feminine = la / le. The rest comes with practice.
4. The indefinite article: un, uno, una, un'
Watch out: "un amico" (masculine) is written WITHOUT an apostrophe, but "un'amica" (feminine) WITH one.

With singular relatives, the possessive is used WITHOUT the article: "mia sorella" (my sister), "mio padre" (my father). In the plural or with "mamma / papà", the article comes back: "i miei genitori", "la mia mamma".
"Il nipote" means both grandson and nephew. Pietro is Graziella's "nipote".
"C'è" = there is (one thing), "ci sono" = there are (several):
My sister is in the photo.
My parents are in the photo.
"Sei" means both "6" and "you are". The context tells you which.
My parents have a big house.
